content: To get us started, in plain language, what does Evergreen Grounds Co. do or plan to do for its customers day to day?
We run a Landscaping Company with two lines of business: recurring lawn maintenance for homeowners and tree/shrub service jobs for local businesses.

Evergreen Grounds Co. is a service business that will provide on-site landscaping services in the Jacksonville area, with one side focused on recurring residential lawn maintenance (mowing, edging, basic yard upkeep for homeowners) and the other side focused on more specialized tree and shrub work for local commercial properties, charging per visit or per job. You’ll generate revenue by performing these services at customer locations on a scheduled or as-needed basis; you’re not selling physical products or running a retail location. It is not an online-only or DIY product business. Does that description sound accurate?
yes

Based on the start date you provided, I'm treating this as pre-revenue for planning context; if that's off, tell me and I'll adjust.  

Since you mentioned both homeowners and local businesses, would you like to keep these as two separate lines of business for planning (residential lawn maintenance vs. commercial tree/shrub work), or treat everything together as one combined landscaping operation?
yes

Got it, we’ll treat them as two separate lines of business: recurring residential lawn maintenance, and commercial tree/shrub service jobs.  

For the residential lawn maintenance side, when a homeowner hires you and pays you once, what would you consider “one unit” of service—would that be one standard lawn visit to a single property (mowing, edging, basic cleanup) on a given day?
Two units: (1) one lawn maintenance visit, and (2) one tree/shrub service job.

Perfect, we’ll track two units across your two lines of business: one residential lawn maintenance visit, and one tree/shrub service job.  

For the residential lawn maintenance visit: in a typical visit to a homeowner’s property, what’s included in that one visit (for example, mowing, edging, blowing off hard surfaces, basic debris pickup), and about how long does a standard visit usually take on an average-sized yard?
A lawn visit covers mowing, edging, and cleanup; a tree/shrub job covers trimming and hauling.
That makes sense, thank you. For the residential lawn maintenance visit specifically, what do you expect to charge on average for one standard visit to a typical homeowner’s yard?
A lawn visit covers mowing, edging, and cleanup; a tree/shrub job covers trimming and hauling.
Understood on what each service includes. For pricing, what do you expect to charge on average for one standard residential lawn maintenance visit to a typical homeowner’s yard?
A lawn visit covers mowing, edging, and cleanup; a tree/shrub job covers trimming and hauling.

I have what’s included in each service, but I can’t complete the planning without a dollar amount; I’ll propose specific pricing so you only need to say yes or adjust. For a standard residential lawn maintenance visit (mowing, edging, cleanup), can we use $55 per visit as your average price?
120 per lawn visit and 500 per tree/shrub job.

Thanks, that’s clear and very helpful.  

For the residential lawn maintenance side: in a fully booked week with your planned crew and equipment, about how many of those $120 lawn visits do you think you can realistically complete?
25 lawn visits and 6 tree/shrub jobs per week.

Great, that gives us a solid starting point for capacity.  

Because you’re doing the work at customer properties, I’m assuming customers receive both services as on-site service at their location (you or your crew drive to the property, do the work there, and then leave). Is that accurate?
On-site service at the customer property with our crew and equipment.

Got it, on-site service at the customer property with your crew and equipment for both units.  

Here’s how I’ll assume fulfillment works: you (and/or a small crew) handle all lawn visits and tree/shrub jobs yourselves, traveling to each property with your equipment; lawn visits are typically done on a set weekly or biweekly schedule, while tree/shrub jobs are booked in advance and completed on the scheduled day or within a few days of booking, and the main thing that limits how much you can do in a week is crew labor hours and travel time rather than demand or software systems. Does this look right?
yes

Since you’re based in Jacksonville and doing on-site work, I’ll assume you’re mainly serving the local Jacksonville area rather than all of Florida or beyond; would you describe your service area as local within the Jacksonville metro, or something broader like regional across multiple Florida cities?
Local.

Since you’re local, I’ll propose we treat your coverage as the Jacksonville metro centered around your business address—specifically Jacksonville and nearby areas like Orange Park and Jacksonville Beach; does “Jacksonville, Orange Park, Jacksonville Beach” capture your normal service area, or would you add/remove any nearby cities?

{{fact:business.name}} operates as a local, on-site lawn and landscape service focused on two main paid units of work: recurring residential lawn maintenance visits for homeowners and scheduled tree/shrub service jobs for local businesses. Work is fulfilled by the owner and a small crew using their own equipment, traveling to each customer property in the Jacksonville metro (Jacksonville, Orange Park, Jacksonville Beach). Residential lawn maintenance is delivered on a weekly or biweekly route schedule, each {{fact:ops.unit_name}} including mowing, edging, and cleanup, typically booked as ongoing recurring service. Tree and shrub jobs for commercial clients are scoped and scheduled in advance, then completed on the appointed day or within a few days, including trimming and hauling. Capacity is primarily constrained by labor (crew time, drive time between jobs, and daylight/weather) rather than systems, with demand growth as the main lever for scaling toward the planned {{fact:ops.units_per_week_capacity}} units per week at the agreed {{fact:ops.unit_price}} per unit. Standard local requirements for a {{fact:ops.legal_entity}} field service contractor—such as any required business licensing, landscape/tree service permits, hauling/disposal compliance, and appropriate liability and commercial auto insurance—are assumed to be incorporated into operations, recognizing that exact regulations and permit needs depend on the specific Florida and Jacksonville-area jurisdictional rules.
